scenes.title: "Drowsy but awake" skips two conditions
scenes.voice: Put her down drowsy but awake. You've heard it a hundred times. You tried it. Your baby screamed the moment she touched the crib. And you rocked her to sleep in your arms again, feeling like you'd failed. You didn't fail. This advice skips two conditions, and in this video I'll show you both.

scenes.title: It describes the result, not the first step
scenes.sub: "My baby can't do it" and "I'm doing it wrong" are both untrue
scenes.voice: Hi, I'm Tetiana, a baby sleep consultant. I've worked with more than five thousand families over eight years. The advice drowsy but awake describes the result, not the first step. It's what falling asleep looks like once everything is already set up. But moms get it as an instruction for tonight. And when the baby cries, mom concludes: my baby can't do this, or I'm doing something wrong. Both conclusions are wrong.

scenes.title: Tired enough for her own norm
scenes.body: Not a chart from the internet, her own number
scenes.voice: To fall asleep on her own, a child has to come to the crib with enough sleep pressure, meaning tired enough for her own norm. That norm is individual: how many hours a day this child sleeps and how long she stays awake. If she's under-tired, she simply can't fall asleep without help. If she's overtired, she's running on adrenaline, and she won't fall asleep either. So the first step isn't in the crib. It's in the daytime schedule. And that's not a chart from the internet. It's her own number.

scenes.title: Don't skip a level
scenes.voice: Condition two. Don't skip a level.

scenes.title: Three levels of falling asleep
scenes.body: 1 with an association · 2 with minimal help · 3 on her own
scenes.voice: Falling asleep has three levels. Level one: with an association, at the breast, with a bottle, in your arms, in motion. Level two: with minimal help, mom nearby, a hand, a quiet sound. Level three: on her own. Drowsy but awake is a jump straight from level one to level three. Skipping a level breaks trust. The child doesn't understand what's happening, and she protests. Protest here isn't failure. It's a signal that a rung on the ladder was skipped.

scenes.title: How to go through level two
scenes.voice: So how do you go through level two?

scenes.title: Put her down as she dives into sleep
scenes.body: Hand and shhh · pick up if she protests · up to 5 tries
scenes.voice: Once the schedule is in place, put your baby in the crib at the moment she's already diving into sleep: eyes drifting, movements slowing. Keep your hand on her and a quiet shhh. If she protests, pick her up, calm her, and as soon as she's diving in again, put her down. Up to five tries per bedtime. After the fifth, you can help her fall asleep the usual way, and that's not a defeat. This way she learns step by step, not through tears.

scenes.title: Readiness bells
scenes.body: Has she ever fallen asleep without the usual condition?
scenes.voice: How do you know your child is ready? Look for times she fell asleep without her usual condition: in the car, at grandma's, turning away from the breast and drifting off. I call these readiness bells. She already wants to fall asleep differently, but doesn't know how yet. Write those moments down. They're your starting point. And remember: I use full independent sleep methods from four and a half to five months.

scenes.title: Protest isn't failure
scenes.sub: The first day is always the hardest
scenes.voice: Many moms give up after the first evening with tears. But a new way of falling asleep is like a new path through the grass. The first day is always the hardest, then it gets easier. One bad evening after a few good ones is what a new skill normally looks like, not a step back. If one time you had to help more, next time you just take one more small step forward.

scenes.title: No crying it out
scenes.sub: In deep stress a child doesn't learn, she only feels scared
scenes.voice: And this is important: all of this is without crying it out. If your child is hysterical, turning red, not responding to your voice, stop any attempt. In deep stress a child doesn't learn, she only feels scared. Your calm matters more than any technique. If you're unsure and scared, better not to start tonight. First get some sleep and agree on one strategy as a family. Your child feels your confidence.

scenes.title: Your step this week
scenes.body: What she falls asleep with now, and any readiness bells
scenes.voice: If drowsy but awake didn't work for you, it isn't about you, and it isn't about your child. First sleep pressure and the schedule, then minimal help, and only then falling asleep on her own. Your step this week: write down what your child falls asleep with now, and whether there have been any readiness bells. Start from the next rung, not the last one.
